claims.text: Thermomechanical processing combined with a secondary stabilization method will produce a fine-grained, thermally stable FeNiCrCoCu coating.
A secondary grain-boundary-pinning mechanism will suppress high-temperature grain coarsening.
A finer grain size produces increased grain-boundary density.
Grain boundaries in the fine-grained coating act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Increasing grain-boundary density will reduce dislocation mobility during high-temperature sliding.
Reduced dislocation mobility will diminish microscopic plastic deformation during sliding.
Reduced dislocation mobility will decrease crack nucleation and propagation under sliding contact.
Decreased crack nucleation and propagation will enhance high-temperature wear resistance.
The refined and stabilized coating will have a lower wear rate than the coarse-grained baseline coating at 600–800 °C.
The refined and stabilized coating will exhibit less localized microscopic plastic deformation than the coarse-grained baseline at 600–800 °C.
Significant grain growth during testing may eliminate the predicted reductions in wear and deformation.
The refined grains may have limited long-term stability under repeated sliding and thermal cycling.

contradictions.description: The boundary treats loss of the refined structure as failure of the stabilization intervention that can explain absent performance gains, whereas the falsification rule says failure to maintain the finer structure itself falsifies the dislocation-hindrance hypothesis. Failure to achieve or retain the mediator is not by itself a decisive test of the mediator's proposed effect.
